title: SLO Tactical Response and Capacity Arbitration Framework
author: Lena Chen
content:
Overview

## Purpose
This document defines a tactical response framework for SLO burn, error-budget arbitration, and immediate capacity decisions during incidents. It covers: identification, automated mitigation, manual capacity arbitration, temporary routing/degradation policies, escalation, and post-incident SLO remediation. The goal is to standardize decisions so product impact is minimized while preserving long-term reliability economics.

## Scope
- Applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated capacity, private deployments) served by the Redwood runtime.
- Operational applicability: oncall engineers, SRE shift lead, capacity owners, product stewards, and incident commanders.
- Excludes planned capacity upgrades (handled by capacity-planning playbooks).

## Definitions
- SLO: Service-level objective defined as P99 latency and success rate per route or model.
- Error budget: allowed fraction of SLO violations in a rolling 30-day window.
- Burn rate: rate at which the error budget is consumed relative to expected rate.
- Arbitration: manual decision to reallocate capacity, throttle tenants, or flip routing policies.

## High-level Principles
1. Protect correctness over performance when a choice must be made (fail closed vs return degraded results).
2. Prefer automated mitigations first; escalate to manual arbitration only when automation cannot restore SLO within defined windows.
3. Make temporary capacity and throttling changes visible to product teams with guardrails and expiration timestamps.
4. All arbitration actions require evidence captured in the incident timeline and must be validated in the post-incident review.

## SLO Tiers and Example Thresholds
Use these tiers as the primary signal for escalation. Teams may add product-specific qualifiers.

| Tier | SLO Metric | Target | Error Budget (30d) | Burn Rate trigger |
|------|-----------:|--------:|-------------------:|------------------:|
| Critical | P99 end-to-end latency (api.v1.generate) | <= 250ms | 0.1% | > 10x over 1h |
| High     | Success rate (route) | >= 99.9% | 0.1% | > 6x over 2h |
| Standard | Tail latency (model-serving KV cache) | P95 <= 120ms | 0.5% | > 3x over 4h |

Note: Teams should map product routes to the nearest tier in the SLO registry.

## Automated Triggers and First Responders
- Alerting rules in the SLO observability pipeline:
  - burn_rate > threshold for rolling window -> page oncall SRE + Slack alert to #slo-alerts.
  - queue depth > scaling threshold -> autoscaler attempt + alert if scale fails for 5m.
- First responder actions (automated / scripted):
  1. Validate telemetry: check the SLO time series and request traces for anomalies.
  2. Activate automated fallback policy if configured (model variant fallback or degraded execution path).
  3. Trigger a short-lived scale-up (elastic reservoir) and watch for SLO improvement for 10 minutes.

## Capacity Arbitration Matrix (Quick reference)
If automated mitigations do not bring the service under thresholds within the observation window, follow the matrix below. Each row is an escalation path; pick the earliest applicable step.

| Condition | Action | Owner | Max Duration (temporary) | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| Burn rate 6-10x for 30-60m | Open arbitration ticket, apply targeted tenant throttles (priority-based) | SRE Shift Lead | 2h | error budget heatmap + traffic shard map |
| Burn rate >10x for 15-30m | Route traffic away from overloaded region/model variant (regional fallback) | Oncall + Runtime Ops | 1h | routing decision record + capacity headroom snapshot |
| Autoscaler failing to provision | Evict non-critical background workloads and apply emergency allocation | Infra Capacity Owner | 4h | instance provisioning logs + eviction list |
| Sustained high latency across tiers | Pause non-essential features (embedding batch jobs, diagnostics) | Product Stewards + SRE | 24h | feature toggle audit + customer impact note |

## Step-by-step Runbook: Elevated SLO Burn (oncall)
1. Acknowledge the page and set incident severity based on the SLO tier.
2. Collect evidence:
   - SLO burn rate dashboard link (copy snapshot).
   - Top 10 request traces grouped by route/model.
   - Recent deployment/rollout history for the last 6 hours.
3. Execute automated mitigations (see "Automated Triggers").
4. If burn persists after the observation window, follow Capacity Arbitration Matrix for the matching condition.
5. Document any manual throttles or routing changes in the arbitration ticket with TTLs and rollback instructions.
6. Notify product stakeholders via the incident channel with the specific customer-impacting routes and expected timeline.
7. Reassess every 15 minutes until SLOs return to target or a longer-term remediation path is approved.

## Temporary Throttle Policy (how to throttle safely)
- Throttles must be applied at the token/request priority layer, not at the firewall. Prefer soft throttles first.
- Example token-priority throttle command (CLI):

redwoodctl throttle apply --tenant tenant-123 --route api.v1.generate --rate 50rps --until "2026-01-12T15:00:00Z" --reason "SLO arbitration: elevated burn"

- Required metadata: issued_by, ttl, reason, expected_recovery_indicator, rollback_command.

## Routing and Degradation Playbook
- Preferred strategies (ranked):
  1. Regional fallback -> move traffic to nearest-region replica with capacity margin.
  2. Model variant fallback -> switch requests to quantized/cheaper variant with acceptable quality degradation.
  3. Structured response -> return partial responses with explicit confidence tags for costly steps.
- Each strategy must include validation hooks: canary 1% traffic, A/B loss check, and rollback rule if error budget burn increases.

## Escalation Matrix and Contacts
- Level 0: Oncall SRE (first page) -> expected response 5 minutes.
- Level 1: SRE Shift Lead (second page) -> expected response 15 minutes.
- Level 2: Infra Capacity Owner + Product Steward -> expected response 30 minutes.
- Level 3: Executive escalation (only after >4h unresolved or customer SLA breach) -> CC: Head of Reliability, Customer Success.

Contact list (primary):
- Oncall SRE: oncall@redwood.example (P1 route via PagerDuty)
- SRE Shift Lead: sre-shift@redwood.example
- Capacity Owner: infra-capacity@redwood.example
- Product Steward: product-steward@redwood.example

## Observability Checklist (must attach to arbitration ticket)
- Burn rate timeseries (30d, 7d, 1d, 1h).
- Per-tenant contribution to burn (top 10).
- Autoscaler events and errors.
- Per-model KV cache hit rate and cold-start counts.
- Recent kernel scheduling anomalies or OOM events (if any).

## Incident Review Evidence Standard (what to capture)
1. Timeline of actions with UTC timestamps (all automated + manual).
2. Arbitration ticket with TTL, issued_by, and rollback_command.
3. Snapshots of capacity headroom, routing maps, and tenant throttle lists.
4. Post-change validation results (canary metrics).
5. Customer impact summary: routes affected, expected request loss, mitigation level.

## Post-incident Remediation Steps
- Short (<24h) incidents: update SLO dashboard annotations, rotate TTL expirations, and run a 1-hour retrospective with the oncall and owners.
- Medium (24h-7d) incidents: schedule a technical RCA with infra and runtime teams; identify configuration or autoscaler changes.
- Long (>7d) incidents or repeated patterns: create a cross-team reliability initiative with milestones (owned in Jira). Include: model-variant evaluation, autoscaler tuning, and capacity reserve adjustments.

Required follow-ups (examples):
- Add tenant to traffic shaping whitelist to prevent disproportionate burn.
- Create canary load tests that reproduce the burst profile observed.
- Adjust SLO tier mapping if product patterns have changed.

## Governance: When is Arbitration Allowed
- Arbitration may be applied only if both:
  a) error budget burn persists after automated mitigations for the defined observation window; and
  b) capacity owner and SRE shift lead approve the arbitration ticket.
- All arbitrations must have TTL <= 24 hours unless explicitly extended by Infra Director.

## Metrics for Measuring Playbook Effectiveness
- Mean time from burn_rate_alert -> mitigation applied. Target: < 10 minutes.
- Fraction of arbitration actions with explicit rollback commands. Target: 100%.
- Reduction in average time to SLO recovery when arbitration applied vs not applied. Target: >= 30% improvement.

## Appendix A — Example Alerting Rule (Prometheus-style JSON snippet)
{
  "expr": "increase(slo_error_budget_consumed_total[1h]) / slo_error_budget_total > 0.1",
  "for": "10m",
  "labels": {"severity": "page"},
  "annotations": {"summary": "High SLO burn rate for {{ $labels.route }}"}
}

## Appendix B — Incident Ticket Template (copy into Jira)
- Title: [Arbitration] <service> elevated burn - <date>
- Priority: P1 / P2 based on SLO tier
- Fields to fill: evidence links, mitigation steps, issued_by, TTL, rollback_command, stakeholder_notify_list

## Ownership and Review Cadence
- SRE: maintain the framework and run biweekly drills.
- Capacity Owners: review and approve emergency allocation rules quarterly.
- Product Stewards: validate route-to-tier mappings during each roadmap cycle.
